title: Inner twists of finite-field Frobenius have finitely many fixed points
statement: Let $k$ be a finite field [def-weil-field, def-weil-finite-field-q-elements], let $q=|k|$, and let $\bar k$ be an algebraic closure [def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $A$ be an affine group scheme of finite type over $k$ [def-sc-group-scheme, def-weil-affine-spectrum, def-weil-finite-type-morphism], with coordinate algebra $C=\Gamma(A,\mathcal O_A)$. Identify $A(\bar k)$ with the $k$-algebra homomorphisms $C\to\bar k$, and write $\sigma(u)(c)=u(c)^q$ for arithmetic Frobenius [def-weil-frobenius-substitution]. For every $x\in A(\bar k)$, the set $\{u\in A(\bar k):x\sigma(u)x^{-1}=u\}$ is finite. Neither smoothness nor connectedness nor commutativity of $A$ is assumed.

source.place: Theorem 17.96, proof, printed p.383: f(g)=xF(g)x^{-1}, f^m=Int(y)F^m, and raising to the finite order of y. Specialize F to finite-field Frobenius; the fixed-point finiteness argument does not use connectedness or smoothness.

proof.text: By [lem-pc-affine-finite-type-algebra], $C$ is a finite-type $k$-algebra. Choose generators $c_1,\ldots,c_t$ as in [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra]. Evaluation $E:A(\bar k)\to\bar k^t$, $u\mapsto(u(c_i))_i$, is injective: if $u,v$ agree on the generators, then for every $c=P(c_1,\ldots,c_t)$ with coefficients in $k$, $u(c)=P(u(c_1),\ldots,u(c_t))=P(v(c_1),\ldots,v(c_t))=v(c)$. This also covers $t=0$.

source.place: Tag 01T2, lemma-locally-finite-type-characterize: apply to the whole affine scheme; write out determination by generators.

proof.text: Each $x(c_i)$ is algebraic over $k$ by [def-weil-algebraic-closure]. By [lem-weil-pbc-algebraic-generators-finite-extension], $L=k(x(c_1),\ldots,x(c_t))\subseteq\bar k$ is finite-dimensional over $k$. A basis of length $d$ gives a bijection $k^d\to L$ by taking coordinates, so $L$ is a finite set (of size $q^d$). All values $x(c)$ lie in $L$, by the polynomial expressions of step 1.

source.place: Tag 09GH, lemma-algebraic-finitely-generated; Milne Theorem 17.96 proof, choosing a Frobenius power fixing x.

proof.text: The field automorphism $\varphi:z\mapsto z^q$ of [def-weil-frobenius-substitution] sends $L$ into itself and is injective there. On the finite set $L$ it is bijective. Among its powers as maps $L\to L$ two coincide, say $\varphi^a=\varphi^b$ with $0\leq a<b$; cancellation of the permutation $\varphi^a$ gives $\varphi^m=1$ for $m=b-a>0$. Thus $\sigma^m(x)=x$. Here $\sigma$ acts by postcomposing a point with $\varphi$; it preserves multiplication and inverse because the multiplication, inverse and identity of [def-sc-group-scheme] are morphisms over $k$, hence commute with change of the coefficient algebra by the $k$-automorphism $\varphi$. Iterating coordinates gives $\sigma^n(u)(c)=u(c)^{q^n}$.

source.place: Theorem 17.96, printed p.383, sentence choosing a Frobenius endomorphism fixing x; functor-of-points naturality and the finite permutation argument written out.

proof.text: For every $n\geq1$, put $H_n=\{u:\sigma^n(u)=u\}$. By [lem-weil-unique-subfield-of-closure], $K_n=\{z\in\bar k:z^{q^n}=z\}$ is a finite field with $q^n$ elements. The injection $E$ of step 1 restricts to an injection $H_n\hookrightarrow K_n^t$, since $\sigma^n(u)=u$ forces $u(c_i)^{q^n}=u(c_i)$ for every $i$. Therefore $H_n$ is finite. It is a subgroup: $\sigma^n(uv)=\sigma^n(u)\sigma^n(v)$ and $\sigma^n(u^{-1})=\sigma^n(u)^{-1}$, so fixed points contain the identity and are closed under products and inverses.

source.place: Definition 17.95 and following paragraph, printed p.382: Frobenius has finitely many fixed points; explicit affine-coordinate count using the existing finite-subfield lemma.

proof.text: Put $f(u)=x\sigma(u)x^{-1}$ and $y_n=x\sigma(x)\cdots\sigma^{n-1}(x)$ for $n\geq1$. Induction gives $f^n(u)=y_n\sigma^n(u)y_n^{-1}$. The base $n=1$ is the definition. For the induction step, apply $f$ to the formula: the conjugating element becomes $x\sigma(y_n)=x\sigma(x)\cdots\sigma^n(x)=y_{n+1}$. For $y=y_m$, the equality $\sigma^m(x)=x$ implies $\sigma^m(\sigma^i(x))=\sigma^i(x)$ for every $i$, and hence $\sigma^m(y)=y$, so $y\in H_m$.

source.place: Theorem 17.96 proof, printed p.383: the direct calculation f^m=Int(y)F^m, expanded by induction.

proof.text: The powers $1,y,y^2,\ldots$ lie in the finite group $H_m$. Two coincide, $y^a=y^b$ for $a<b$; cancellation gives $y^r=1$ with $r=b-a>0$. Since $\sigma^m(y)=y$, induction on $j\geq0$ gives $(f^m)^j(u)=y^j\sigma^{mj}(u)y^{-j}$. At $j=0$ this is the identity; composing with $f^m$ replaces $y^j$ by $y\sigma^m(y^j)=y^{j+1}$. Consequently $f^{mr}=\sigma^{mr}$.

source.place: Theorem 17.96 proof, printed p.383: the second iterate identity and killing the finite-order conjugating element.

proof.text: If $f(u)=u$, induction gives $f^s(u)=u$ for every $s\geq0$. In particular $\sigma^{mr}(u)=f^{mr}(u)=u$. Since $mr\geq1$, every point in question belongs to the finite set $H_{mr}$ from step 4. A subset of a finite set is finite. All constructions used the affine finite-type coordinate algebra and the group laws only; they apply equally to nonreduced and disconnected group schemes.

source.place: Theorem 17.96 proof, printed p.383, last sentence: fixed points of f lie in the fixed points of its Frobenius iterate.

proof_origin.place: Theorem 17.96 proof, printed pp.382–383: its iteration argument, with affine-coordinate finiteness and finite-field definition-of-point details supplied for arbitrary affine finite-type group schemes.

It touches only the item and its report, has no new nodes, and the statement is byte-identical to the base copy in clones/side-live (unsplit, no proof). The seven steps follow Milne iAG2017, Theorem 17.96 proof (printed p.383) and the paragraph after Def 17.95 (p.382): f(g)=xF(g)x^{-1}; a power F^m fixes x; f^m=Int(y)F^m with y=x·F(x)···F^{m-1}(x); f^{mr}=F^{mr} once r is the order of y; the fixed points of f then sit inside a finite Frobenius-fixed set. I re-derived both inductions, including the order of the noncommuting factors (x·σ(y_n)=y_{n+1}; f^m(y^jσ^{mj}u y^{-j})=y^{j+1}…). The cited statements say what the steps take from them: lem-pc-affine-finite-type-algebra gives a finite-type coordinate ring C; def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra gives polynomial generators, so evaluation on generators is injective; the algebraic-generators lemma (a Mathlib leaf) makes L finite; def-weil-frobenius-substitution gives φ as a k-automorphism of the closure, and σ is a group map by naturality of the functor of points (def-sc-group-scheme); clause 1 of lem-weil-unique-subfield-of-closure says K_n has q^n elements. Edge cases checked: t=0, x=e, mu_p, G_m, and finite noncommutative constant groups. The fixed-point argument never uses smoothness, connectedness, reducedness or commutativity, so the general statement is true.
